why: Canary 1.1 introduces a sustained 5xx regression on the checkout path. Evidence from the dashboard: canary served 10 5xx vs 0 for stable (canary 0.41% overall vs stable 0.00%). All 10 failures land on /checkout: canary /checkout 10/483 = 2.07% err vs stable /checkout 0/1455 = 0.00%. /browse (0/1236 vs 0/3695) and /search (0/736 vs 0/2209) are clean on both versions, so the fault is isolated to the highest-value route rather than spread across the service. The over-time table shows canary 5xx of 1, 3, 3, 3 across the 0-30s, 30-60s, 60-90s and 90-120s windows while stable stays at 0 in every window, so the errors persist for the full 120s instead of being confined to the first window the way a cold-start or warm-up blip would be. Latency is not a factor and does not argue against rollback: canary p50/p95/p99 match stable overall (28/96/105 vs 32/94/104) and per-route (/browse 22/27/28 vs 21/27/28, /search 46/58/60 vs 46/58/60, /checkout 83/104/106 vs 82/104/106), and canary p95 stays within 1-5ms of stable in every window. Judgement: with 0 failures observed in 1455 stable checkout requests, a 2.07% failure rate over 483 canary checkout requests is very unlikely to be sampling noise, and promoting to 100% would imply roughly 1 in 50 customer checkouts failing on the revenue-critical path. Given that a bad promote hurts customers while a bad rollback only delays a release, the asymmetry favours rolling back and fixing the checkout error before retrying the canary.
